transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, then we'll jump into the KMS and audit checklist that Alex prepared.
[00:12] Sofia Rami: Hi, Sofia here from Orbitalk. We have Daniel, Priya and Luca on the line too.
[00:17] Daniel Kim: Daniel - Security.
[00:19] Priya Nair: Priya - PM.
[00:21] Luca Marino: Luca - DevOps.
[00:23] Maya Chen: Great. Alex, you want to kick us off with the integration summary?
[00:28] Alex Ruiz: Sure. So, high-level: Redwood's marketplace listing needs to support two distribution modes for partners — managed listing (hosted) and connector (on-prem/VPC). In your case Orbitalk wants a hybrid where customers can subscribe via marketplace but deploy a private connector in their VPC, and we surface billing/entitlement. The main technical asks today are: confirmation of KMS/HSM compatibility, audit log semantics and retention, and a short runbook for helm/operator deployment.
[00:50] Sofia Rami: That's accurate. We also have compliance constraints: keys must be customer-managed in their KMS for certain accounts, and audit trails must be immutable for 365 days.
[01:02] Daniel Kim: To add: we need to confirm that Redwood can integrate with AWS KMS and Google Cloud KMS, and we have a couple of customers on Azure Key Vault as well. For FIPS/HSM-backed keys, we want to know the supported modes.
[01:18] Alex Ruiz: Right. On Redwood side we have an abstracted KMS interface. For hosted customers Redwood can manage keys or integrate to customer KMS via external key encryption (EKM). For Dedicated and Private deploy modes we support customer-provided KMS using either native KMS API or a KMS proxy in the VPC. Our documented patterns cover AWS KMS, GCP KMS and Azure Key Vault; HSMs via KMIP are supported in our private package but need a runbook.
[01:43] [crosstalk]
[01:44] Priya Nair: When you say "EKM" can you spell out how the private key never leaves the HSM?
[01:49] Alex Ruiz: Sure — the flow we recommend is envelope encryption: the model artifacts and token caches are encrypted with a data key, the data key is wrapped by the customer KMS using a wrapping key that never leaves the HSM. For KMIP/HSM we do remote signing calls to the HSM — Redwood's runtime keeps only the wrapped key. There are latency implications which we should benchmark.
[02:10] Maya Chen: Jordan, can you add the product note about fallback behavior?
[02:13] Jordan Patel: Yeah. Important to note: if KMS is unavailable, our fallback is to use a cached encrypted key that auto-expires and we push requests to a degraded mode with limited scale. We've got policy knobs for TTL and canary fallback. For customers with strict compliance, we recommend a synchronous KMS call on startup and tighter health checks so degraded mode is not used.
[02:33] Daniel Kim: That's concerning — we can't allow a fallback that uses Redwood-managed keys for our regulated accounts.
[02:39] Alex Ruiz: Understood. We can gate fallback behavior via account-level policy. For your regulated tenant profiles we'll require a hard fail if KMS is unreachable, and we'll document that in the listing as a requirements checklist.
[02:49] Luca Marino: On the helm side, what does the chart expect? Do you need a sidecar/proxy for KMS or do we inject credentials as secrets? What's the recommended practice for our security team?
[02:59] Alex Ruiz: The recommended is to deploy a small KMS-proxy sidecar inside the cluster that performs strictly local KMS calls over private subnet to the customer's KMS endpoint. We provide a sample Helm chart with an optional kms-proxy subchart. If you prefer native cloud IAM, we also support IRSA/Workload Identity bindings. We'll share both examples.
[03:18] Priya Nair: For marketplace listing metadata, we need a short checklist: minimal required fields, required compliance attestations, logos, and a sample privacy notice.
[03:27] Maya Chen: I'll send the marketplace checklist after the call. We'll also add the listing's "deployment modes" flags so it's clear whether a buyer can choose managed vs connector.
[03:36] [00:03:40] Sofia Rami: Quick Q on audit logs — do you capture token-level events? We need to show per-request user identity for certain endpoints.
[03:45] Alex Ruiz: We have structured audit logs for request metadata (request id, timestamp, model, route, token counts, authenticated principal). For Private, logs can be either stored in Redwood cloud or forwarded to a customer SOC via syslog/HTTP/S3. We support immutable append-only logs if you enable our audit sink to a customer-managed S3 with object lock.
[04:07] Daniel Kim: Does Redwood hash PII before writing to logs? We prefer hashing for anything that might be sensitive.
[04:13] Alex Ruiz: We can support a sanitizer step where PII is masked or hashed before logs are emitted. That is configurable in the runtime. We'll include the sanitizer config in the runbook.
[04:24] Maya Chen: Can we walk through a sample flow? Luca, do you want to share your current sandbox constraints so Alex can map the steps?
[04:31] Luca Marino: Sure. Our sandbox is a single VPC with two private subnets, no outbound internet except through a NAT. We want the connector to live in those private subnets and talk to customer KMS via endpoint. Also, marketplace entitlement will push an SSO token back to the connector to validate license. We need to ensure the connector doesn't need inbound ports open from Redwood.
[04:56] Alex Ruiz: That's fine. Our connector supports outbound-only connections to Redwood control plane over TLS, using mutual TLS if you prefer. Entitlement checks happen over an authenticated outbound connection; the connector pulls config, validates entitlements with a signed JWT. No inbound ports required.
[05:12] Priya Nair: About the signed JWT — who holds the private key that signs it?
[05:17] Jordan Patel: For marketplace flows, Redwood signs a short-lived token using our platform key and we provide provenance metadata. For self-hosted deployments you can configure the connector to accept tokens issued by a partner STS or Redwood — we'll include both flows in the listing.
[05:30] [00:05:36] Sofia Rami: Are there known scale/latency numbers when envelope encryption is used with external KMS on every session creation? We have customers with bursty auth patterns.
[05:41] Alex Ruiz: Per-session synchronous KMS wraps are heavier. Typical envelope wrap/unwrap latencies are 30-120ms depending on region and HSM. Our recommended pattern is to cache wrapped data keys with short TTL and only do sync unwrap during key rotation or first boot. We'll include a benchmark spreadsheet.
[05:58] Daniel Kim: We'll want that benchmark. Also, we need to know if the signed JWT verification is done locally — like does the connector do a CRL/ocsp check?
[06:07] Alex Ruiz: Connector verifies signature locally and optionally checks revocation via a JWKS endpoint; we support punched CRL requests outbound to the JWKS origin. It's configurable.
[06:18] Luca Marino: On packaging: we run various Kubernetes flavors incl. EKS, AKS and on-prem OpenShift. Does the Helm chart require specific CRI or kernel modules?
[06:27] Alex Ruiz: No kernel modules required. We support standard OCI images and the chart is tested on EKS/OCP/AKS. For on-prem we provide a lite operator for lifecycle and upgrades. We'll surface the operator in the partner listing as an optional install.
[06:38] Priya Nair: We need the listing to call out the operator's RBAC scopes — security team will review.
[06:43] Maya Chen: Good point. We'll add an RBAC export to the listing artifacts. Alex, can you add a manifest for minimal privileges?
[06:49] Alex Ruiz: Yes, *minimal* RBAC manifests plus a recommended RBAC for production.
[06:52] [00:07:00] Jordan Patel: Another product note — we have a quantization recommendation for connector builds where customers want lower memory. We can publish recommended quant packs for common hardware; it's optional but relevant for on-prem CPU-only guests.
[07:10] Sofia Rami: That could be useful for some of our smaller telco customers. Will those packs change model accuracy or require evals?
[07:16] Jordan Patel: They can slightly affect output distribution. We recommend running evaluation prompts in your UAT harness. Redwood Optimize can provide automated reg checks tied to your prompt sets.
[07:27] Daniel Kim: Back to audit retention — you said object lock on S3. For Azure?
[07:32] Alex Ruiz: For Azure we recommend ADLS Gen2 with immutability policies, or forwarding to Azure Sentinel. We'll include sample sink configs for S3, ADLS, Splunk, and SIEM over Syslog.
[07:46] Luca Marino: For the marketplace listing itself, what is the review timeline? We need to coordinate legal attestation and a security questionnaire.
[07:53] Maya Chen: Typically listing review is 7-14 days if all artifacts are ready. Security questionnaire and pen test reports can add time. For partners with private deployments we usually do a gated preflight that must pass before public listing.
[08:05] Priya Nair: Can we get the preflight checklist?
[08:08] Maya Chen: Yes, I'll attach the preflight doc to the follow-up email.
[08:11] [00:08:20] Sofia Rami: One more technical: how are model updates handled on private connectors — do you push model tarballs or do customers pull from a registry?
[08:19] Alex Ruiz: Both options. For private deployments customers can pull signed model artifacts from a registry (recommended), or Redwood can push compressed deltas via outbound pull. For regulated customers we recommend registry pulls with signed manifests and provenance.
[08:33] Daniel Kim: Do you sign models with a build signature? We need provenance.
[08:36] Jordan Patel: Yes — models/artifacts have a signed manifest and a content-addressable checksum. We'll provide the manifest signing keys and verification steps.
[08:46] Luca Marino: In terms of telemetry, what are the default retention windows? We need 90 days for metrics and 365 for audit logs.
[08:53] Alex Ruiz: Default telemetry is 30 days for detailed token-level traces, 365 days for aggregated metrics; audit logs retention is configurable and we can forward to your storage for 365+ retention. We'll document retention policy knobs.
[09:08] Maya Chen: Alright, let's briefly recap next steps and owners. Alex will produce the KMS checklist and helm snippet. Maya will send marketplace metadata + preflight. Orbitalk will provision sandbox and run the helm deploy. We'll schedule a UAT for week of Mar 29.
[09:23] Priya Nair: Works for me.
[09:24] Sofia Rami: One ask — can Redwood share a short demo video showing the connector deploy and entitlement flow? That will help our SOC and legal teams.
[09:31] Maya Chen: Yes, we have a 6-minute deploy walkthrough video; I'll link it in the follow-up.
[09:36] Daniel Kim: Also, can you include samples of the audit logs with PII masking? We want to validate the sanitizer step.
[09:42] Alex Ruiz: Will do. We'll produce a sample scrubbed log set.
[09:45] [00:09:50] Luca Marino: Small thing — our infra team needs a helm values.yaml example for private registries (no public ecr).
[09:53] Alex Ruiz: We'll include a private registry example in the repo.
[09:56] Maya Chen: Any blockers on timelines?
[09:58] Sofia Rami: Not yet — but Daniel needs to sign off on the KMS fallback policy.
[10:02] Daniel Kim: I'll review the checklist and get back by the 25th.
[10:05] Maya Chen: Perfect. If nothing else we'll wrap. Thanks everyone.
[10:09] Priya Nair: Thanks.
[10:10] Jordan Patel: Thanks all.
[10:11] Alex Ruiz: Bye.
[10:12] [END]
